sets.title: Twenty questions each
sets.transcript:
W: Hey, have you got a minute before maths? It's about the biology test next Tuesday.
M: Sure, I've got five minutes. Are you worried about it?
W: A bit. For the last one, I read my notes three times the night before. I felt ready, and then I sat down in the test and couldn't remember half of it. It was awful.
M: Really? But your notes are always so neat.
W: Neat doesn't help, it turns out. So I want to try something different. What if we each write twenty questions on the chapter, swap them, and answer each other's without looking at the book?
M: Hmm. Honestly, I'd rather we made one big poster together. The heart, the blood vessels, everything in different colours. Drawing things helps me see how they fit.
W: Posters are fun, but think about the test. Nobody hands you a poster. They hand you questions.
M: OK, that's true. But writing twenty questions sounds like a lot of work.
W: It's less work than a poster. And to write a good question, you have to understand the answer first, so that's studying too.
M: Fine, you've convinced me. When do we swap?
W: How about Thursday after school, in the library?
M: Thursday's bad. I've got football practice until five, and the library closes at half past.
W: Then let's swap on Friday at lunch. We can answer them over the weekend and check them together on Monday.
M: Friday at lunch works. Should we split the chapter, or should we both do all of it?
W: Both do all of it. Otherwise you'll only really know your half.
M: Makes sense. And should the questions be hard ones or easy ones?
W: A mix, like the real test. Oh, and write the answers on a separate page, so the other person can't just see them.
M: Got it. I'll start mine tonight, after I finish my history reading.

speakers.S: a teacher giving a short lecture to a high-school class

sets.title: Why sleep helps memory
sets.transcript:
So, with exams coming up, I want to talk about something your parents have probably told you a hundred times. Get a good night's sleep, because it helps you remember what you studied. Lots of people believe this, and as far as scientists can tell, it's actually true. The more interesting question is why it's true, and there are two competing explanations.

The first explanation is fairly simple. While you're awake, new things keep coming into your head. Conversations, messages, songs, whatever. Each new thing can push against the memories you made earlier and make them harder to find. Psychologists call this interference. When you're asleep, almost nothing new comes in. So, on this view, sleep doesn't do anything special. It just gives your memories a quiet place to sit, like a sign on a door that says do not disturb.

The second explanation says sleep is much more active than that. While you sleep, the brain goes back over what you learned during the day and makes those memories stronger. This is called consolidation. So sleep isn't just a quiet room. It's more like a night shift, when workers come in and fix up the day's work.

Now, how could we tell these two apart? Here's the interesting part. Researchers have recorded brain cells in rats while the rats ran through a maze. Certain cells fired in a particular order as a rat moved along the path. Later, when the rat was asleep, those same cells fired again, in roughly the same order, and often faster. It looked as if the sleeping brain was running through the maze again. A quiet room doesn't do that.

An even clearer test was done with people. Volunteers learned where about fifty pictures appeared on a computer screen, and each picture came with its own sound. A cat picture came with a meow, for example. Then they took a nap. While they were in deep sleep, the researchers quietly played the sounds for half of the pictures, too softly to wake anyone up. After the nap, people remembered the locations of those pictures better than the locations of the others.

Think about what each explanation predicts here. If sleep only keeps out new information, then every picture should be protected equally. The sounds shouldn't matter. But they did matter, and only for the pictures they belonged to. That's very hard to explain unless the sleeping brain is actively working on particular memories.

So I'd say the evidence supports the second explanation. That doesn't mean interference counts for nothing. Being awake and busy probably does weaken memories a little. It just can't be the whole story.

Finally, think about the night before a big test, when some of you stay up late studying until two or three in the morning. The common advice your parents gave you about sleep is right. And now you know what your brain would have been doing with those hours.

items.prompt: What did the researchers do while the volunteers were in deep sleep?

They showed the volunteers the pictures again on a screen
They woke the volunteers to ask where the pictures were
They played each sound from the task once again
items.correct_answer: They quietly played the sounds that went with half of the pictures
items.why: While they were in deep sleep, the researchers quietly played the sounds for half of the pictures, too softly to wake anyone up
items.explanation: "They quietly played the sounds that went with half of the pictures" is correct: "While they were in deep sleep, the researchers quietly played the sounds for half of the pictures."

distractor_rationales.reason: "They showed the volunteers the pictures again on a screen" is wrong: the screen was used when they learned; during sleep "the researchers quietly played the sounds".

distractor_rationales.choice: They woke the volunteers to ask where the pictures were
distractor_rationales.reason: "They woke the volunteers to ask where the pictures were" is wrong: the sounds were played "too softly to wake anyone up", and memory was tested "After the nap".

distractor_rationales.choice: They played each sound from the task once again
distractor_rationales.reason: "They played each sound from the task once again" is wrong: they played "the sounds for half of the pictures", not all of them.

items.prompt: What does the picture study suggest about the first explanation?

It explains the result better than the second one does
It was tested by keeping the volunteers awake all night

items.why2: But they did matter, and only for the pictures they belonged to
items.explanation: "It made a prediction that the nap results did not support" is correct: the first explanation means "every picture should be protected equally", but the sounds "did matter, and only for the pictures they belonged to."

distractor_rationales.choice: It correctly predicted which pictures people would remember
distractor_rationales.reason: "It correctly predicted which pictures people would remember" is wrong: it predicts "every picture should be protected equally", yet people remembered some "better than the locations of the others."

distractor_rationales.choice: It explains the result better than the second one does
distractor_rationales.reason: "It explains the result better than the second one does" is wrong: the result is "very hard to explain unless the sleeping brain is actively working on particular memories", and "the evidence supports the second explanation."

distractor_rationales.choice: It was tested by keeping the volunteers awake all night
distractor_rationales.reason: "It was tested by keeping the volunteers awake all night" is wrong: the volunteers slept: "Then they took a nap."
